blocks.text: When the monomer(s) contain C=C bonds, addition polymerisation takes place, for example with ethene, propene and phenylethene (styrene). Usually homopolymers, made of one kind of monomer, are formed, but sometimes two different monomers with double bonds can be polymerised together to give a copolymer, such as the copolymer of ethene and propenoic acid (CH2=CH-COOH).

blocks.alt: Left panel, C=C present means addition: ethene, propene, phenylethene (styrene) and propenoic acid (copolymer with ethene). Right panel, two reactive groups means condensation: -NH2 + -COOH gives a polyamide + H2O; -NH2 + -COCl a polyamide + HCl; -OH + -COOH a polyester + H2O; -OH + -COCl a polyester + HCl.
blocks.caption: Predicting the type of polymerisation from the monomers (original summary of topic 26.4).
blocks.long_description: Look at the functional groups of the monomers. A carbon-carbon double bond can open and add on, so it gives an addition polymer. A pair of groups that react with each other, amine with acid or acyl chloride, or alcohol with acid or acyl chloride, gives a condensation polymer and a small molecule.

blocks.explanation: A polymer made from two (or more) different monomers, e.g. ethene and propenoic acid; a homopolymer has only one kind of monomer.

items: C=C monomers: addition polymers (homopolymers or copolymers).
